etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨yo₂si⟩ → */jəsi/ → /joɕi/ → /joki/ → */joɣi/ → /joi/ → */jiː/ → /iː/
Ultimately a shift from 良い (yoi), classical 良し (yoshi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/idure/ → /id͡zure/ → /izure/
Compound of いづ (izu, interrogative pronoun) + れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives). Long form of いづ (izu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *Etu. Appears in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
The presence of other Old Japanese indefinites beginning with い (i) suggests a possible shared root of い (i, possibly “what” or “which”), as in 如何 (ikaga, “how”), 何処 (izuko, “where”), 幾ら (ikura, “how many, how much”).
Likely cognate with eastern Old Japanese word idu (modern idzu or izu, “where”), still used in modern Japanese as part of the word いずれ (izure, “which”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Attested in The Tale of the Heike (c. 1330).
The kara portion is likely cognate with 絡む (karamu, “to become entangled; start a fight with, to pick a quarrel”), 絡める (karameru, “to entangle, to entwine”), and 絡げる (karageru, “to tie together in a sheave or bunch; to hitch up the hem of a robe or skirt”); with an apparent underlying meaning of entanglement, bunch. The kau portion may be 交う (kau, “to exchange; to mix”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshū of 759.
Apparently a shift from 立ち待ち (tachimachi, “standing and waiting”), the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of compound verb 立ち待つ (tachimatsu, “to wait while standing”), probably from the idea of being at the ready. In older texts, this was always followed by the adverbial particle に (ni) for all senses.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/jamiɡate/ → */jamɡate/ → */jaŋɡate/ → /jaɡate/
Contraction of 止難(やみがて) (yamigate), compound of verb 止(や)む (yamu, “to stop”) + suffix 難(が)て (gate, “difficult”).
First attested around the 10th century.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English hotel, from French hôtel.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tuki tati/ → /t͡suitat͡ɕi/
Originally a compound of 月 (tsuki, “moon; month”) + 立ち (tachi, “standing; starting, occurring”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 立つ (tatsu, “to stand up; to start, to occur”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 一日 (ʔiɪt̚ ȵiɪt̚, literally “one + day”). Compare modern Hakka reading yit-ngit.
The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 一日 (ʔiɪt̚ ȵiɪt̚, literally “one + day”). Compare modern Min Nan reading chi̍t-ji̍t.
This reading uses the goon for the first character and the kan'on for the second character, suggesting a shift in reading after the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 一 (ichi, “one”, on'yomi, or Chinese-derived reading) + 日 (hi, “day”, kun'yomi, or native-Japanese reading).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 一 (hito, “one”) + 日 (hi, “day”). Appears in The Tale of Genji of the early 1000s CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/hitohi/ → /hitohe/ → /hitoe/
Shift in pronunciation from hitohi above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 下(した) (shita, “under”) + 着(ぎ) (-gi, “clothing”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Classical Chinese 主義 /主义 (zhǔyì), attested in the Records of the Grand Historian

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 九 (MC kjuwX). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Borrowed after palatalization occurred in Middle Chinese. Compare literary Hokkien 九 (kiú), Hakka 九 (kiú).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Chinese 九 (MC kjuwX). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare vernacular Hokkien 九 (káu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese from Proto-Japonic *kəkənə.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kokono/ → /kono/
Abbreviation of Old Japanese 九 (kokono, “nine”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 今(いま) (ima, “now”) + に (ni)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese compound 今日 (MC kim nyit). Compare modern Taishanese reading gim¹ ngit⁴.
The goon, so likely the original reading of the term as first borrowed from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/koɲɲit͡ɕi/ → /koɲt͡ɕi/
Shift from konnichi above. Used dialectally in the Shitamachi area of Tokyo since the Edo period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 今日 (MC kim nyit). Compare modern Cantonese reading gam¹ jat⁶.
Change in reading from konnichi, keeping the earlier goon reading kon for 今, but substituting the later kan'on reading jitsu for 日.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 会議(かいぎ) (kaigi, “meeting”) + 室(しつ) (shitsu, “room”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally the -te conjunctive form of Old Japanese verb 統ぶ (subu); compare modern 統べる (suberu, “to gather many things together; to treat many things as a single group”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 化學 /化学 (huàxué, literally “change + study”).
Apparently first cited anywhere in an 1855 text in Chinese, in the diary of noted intellectual Wang Tao. First cited in Japanese in an 1860 translation of a Dutch text by 川(かわ)本(もと)幸(こう)民(みん) (Kawamoto Kōmin).
Superseded older term 舎(せい)密(み) (seimi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Reanalysis of 化(か)学(がく) (kagaku) above, as a compound of 化(ば)け (bake, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 化(ば)ける (bakeru, “to transform”)) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “-logy, -graphy”). Alternative reading sometimes used to differentiate 化(か)学(がく) (kagaku) from 科(か)学(がく) (kagaku, “science”), which it has become an exact homophone of.
First cited to a 1967 novel by 大(おお)原(はら)富(とみ)枝(え) (Ōhara Tomie).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ʑipʉ/ → /ʑiɸu/ → /ʑɨu/ → /ʑuː//ʑiʔ/ → /ʑi~̚/
From Middle Chinese 十 (MC dzyip). Compare literary Hokkien 十 (si̍p).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂wo⟩ → */təwo/ → /towo/ → /toː/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *təwə. The initial to- may be related to the -tu in 五 (itu, “five”), following similar vowel alternations as seen in the numerals for 1-4 and their doubles. Alternatively this word may be related to 撓む (towomu→tōmu, “to bend”), 撓寄る (towoyoru, “to flex”), 撓 (towowo, “bent”), from the way ones fingers bend when counting using them. See the Proto-Japonic reconstruction page for more theories.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from tō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨so₁⟩ → */sʷo/ → /so/
From Old Japanese.
Used in compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Mandarin 十 (shí).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, in turn from Proto-Japonic *siri. Ultimate derivation unknown.
The use as a suffixing element in surnames is of unclear derivation. Many of these surnames may derive from place names, in which case the "behind, the end" sense may be the origin. However, other surnames have no clear geographic derivation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Ainu シㇼ (sir, “place, land, island”). The kanji spelling is an example of ateji.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: wisarapi > wisaraɸi > wisarawi > isarai.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 局 (MC gjowk).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kak- (“to scratch”).
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Cognate with 書く (kaku, “to write”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 朝 (asa, “morning”) + 寝坊 (nebō, “sleeping in, waking late; someone who sleeps in”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *namita.
Attested in the Nihon Shoki with the man'yōgana spelling 那(な)瀰(み)多(た) (namita). The Kojiki and Man'yōshū have 那(な)美(み)多(た) (namita), and the Man'yōshū also has later instances where the 多(た) (ta) was replaced with 太(だ) (da), forming 奈(な)美(み)太(だ) (namida), indicating a phonetic change over time from namita to namida.
Ultimate derivation unknown. There are interesting phonetic and semantic similarities with Thai น้ำตา (nám-dtaa, “tear”, literally “water + eye”), overlapping semantically with Korean 눈물 (nunmul, “tear”, literally “eye + water”), perhaps pointing to an ancient prehistoric borrowing. Alexander Vovin lists it among "naturalized loanwords from Korean". However, such similarities may also be purely accidental.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/namida/ → /nanda/
Alteration of namida above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration of namida or nanda above. Used during the Edo period in the rough informal speech used by the staff and servants of samurai households, and others of lower social rank.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined by Matsumiya Tetsuo in 1908 as a translation of English probability.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 神(かみ) (kami, “deity, god”) + 様(さま) (-sama, honorific suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *penti.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 言(い)い (ii, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 言(い)う (iu)) + 出(だ)す (dasu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/taɴbi/ → /tabi/
Shift in pronunciation from tanbi, the expected regular goon compound reading for the 単皮 spelling, which appears in the Wamyō Ruijushō of 938 CE.
Originally referred to a leather shoe, which could be made from a single (単) animal hide (皮). As footwear in Japan developed, so too did the sense of tabi. The modern sense of a split-toed sock arose from at least the late Kamakura period, around the late 1200s, early 1300s. However, the leather shoe sense was still in use in 1603, as evidenced by the relevant entry in the Nippo Jisho.
The shift in reading was possibly influenced by the regular kun'yomi tabi of the term 旅 (tabi, “travel, voyage, trip”), as the tabi footwear was often worn for travel.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Likely from Old Japanese, compound of 逆(さか) (saka, “reverse”) + 上(のぼ)る (noboru, “ascend, go up”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshu of circa 759 CE, with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 久枳. From Proto-Japonic *kunki.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First cited to the Kojiki of 712.
Further derivation is uncertain.
While a surface analysis might suggest a relation to 鍵 (kagi, “key”) or its cognate 鉤 (kagi, “lock”), Japanese references do not make such a connection. In addition, the oldest uses of derived noun 限り (kagiri, “limitation, bound, extent”) indicate that the initial sense was one of "limitation" in terms of time, in contrast to 極み (kiwami, “limitation, bound, extent”) in terms of space.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Japanese shinjitai. Simplified from 髮 (犮 → 友).
